templates.title: Photography order
templates.description: Book a new photo session or order prints and files from a past shoot.
templates.metaDescription: Take photography orders for new sessions or for prints from a past shoot. Collect the package, date, image numbers, print sizes, delivery and photo usage.
templates.blurb: One form for the two orders a photographer actually gets. New clients choose a session type, package and date; past clients name their gallery and the images they want printed. Everyone is asked how the photos will be used, which settles licensing before it becomes an awkward conversation.

preview.greeting: Hi! Let's get your photography order sorted.
preview.question: Your details first.
preview.next: What are you ordering?

templates.title: Sales performance review
templates.description: A manager's review of one rep: the number, the skills behind it and the support they need next.
templates.metaDescription: Review a salesperson on results, selling skills and habits, not just quota. A miss asks what got in the way; a beat asks what worked, so others can copy it.
templates.blurb: Separates the result from the skills that produced it, so a strong rep in a thin territory is not judged the same as a weak rep in a rich one. The target question decides the follow-up: a miss is asked what got in the way, a beat is asked what worked, and every review ends with one skill to build and the support that would help most.

preview.greeting: Let's review this period. Plan on five minutes, and have their numbers to hand.
preview.question: Which salesperson are you reviewing?
preview.next: Which period does this review cover?

templates.title: 360 degree feedback
templates.description: Feedback on one person from the people around them, with examples, not just scores.
templates.metaDescription: Collect 360 feedback from managers, peers and direct reports with keep, start and stop prompts. Reports also rate leadership, and reviewers choose if they are named.
templates.blurb: Asks every reviewer the same core questions so answers can be compared across managers, peers and direct reports. People who report to the person also rate their leadership, a question the others skip. The keep, start and stop prompts pull out specific examples, and a short follow-up asks for one whenever an answer is too vague to act on.

preview.greeting: You've been asked for feedback on a colleague. Honest and specific is the most useful thing you can give.
preview.question: Who are you giving feedback about?
preview.next: How do you work with them?

templates.title: Staff induction checklist
templates.description: New starters confirm what's done in their first week and flag what's still missing.
templates.metaDescription: A first-week induction checklist for new staff: which steps are done, what is still blocking them, an emergency contact and how ready they feel for week two.
templates.blurb: Sent at the end of a new starter's first week, it turns induction into a checklist the employee confirms themselves. Anyone who says something is blocking them is asked what and who could fix it, so a missing login is sorted on Monday rather than discovered a month later.

preview.greeting: You've made it through week one! A quick check that your induction covered everything.
preview.question: Your name and work email, please.
preview.next: Which team and role have you joined?

templates.title: Ghibli-style art request
templates.description: Take illustration requests for soft, hand-painted anime-style portraits and scenes.
templates.metaDescription: A request form for artists who draw in a soft, hand-painted anime style. Collect the subject, reference photos, mood, colours, format, deadline and usage.
templates.blurb: For artists who take commissions in the gentle, painterly style people associate with classic hand-drawn anime films. Clients who want a portrait, a pet or a place are asked for reference photos, while original scenes get space to describe them. Anyone ordering for business use is asked where it will appear, so the licence is clear before you start.

preview.greeting: Hello! Tell me about the picture you'd like and I'll see how I can bring it to life.
preview.question: What should I call you?
preview.next: What would you like drawn?

templates.title: Employee onboarding
templates.description: Collect what a new starter needs before day one.
templates.metaDescription: Collect what a new hire needs before day one: contact details, start date, kit, emergency contact and a signed handbook, with separate remote and office questions.
templates.blurb: The details that otherwise arrive as five separate emails in the first week: legal name, contact details, kit, an emergency contact and a signature on the handbook. Remote starters get shipping and home-setup questions, office starters pick their site and say how they'll commute, and hybrid starters choose an office and get the home-setup questions too.

preview.greeting: Welcome aboard! A few details so everything's ready on your first day.
preview.question: What's your full legal name?
preview.next: What name and pronouns should we use in the team directory?

templates.title: Employee referral
templates.description: Put a candidate forward with their name, the role and one honest reason they fit.
templates.metaDescription: Let staff refer candidates in a few minutes: who they are, which role and why they fit. Recruiters only contact people who know they've been referred.
templates.blurb: Kept short on purpose, because people stop referring when it feels like paperwork. The candidate's name, the role and one honest reason are enough for a recruiter to act on. When the candidate already knows, the form asks how to reach them; when they don't, it takes the referrer's word that they'll check first, rather than contact details they shouldn't be sharing.

preview.greeting: Know someone great? Put them forward. It only takes a few minutes.
preview.question: First, your name and work email, so we can keep you posted.
preview.next: Which team are you on?

templates.title: Marketing quote
templates.description: Scope a campaign or a retainer well enough to send a real estimate.
templates.metaDescription: Price marketing work without a discovery call: services, goals, timing and budget in one chat. One-off campaigns and monthly retainers get different follow-ups.
templates.blurb: Built for agencies and freelance marketers who are tired of quoting from a one-line enquiry. A one-off campaign is asked about launch date and length, a monthly retainer about who runs marketing today and how long they want to commit, so each estimate starts from the facts that actually move the price.

preview.greeting: Tell us what you're planning and we'll put together an estimate for you.
preview.question: First, who are we preparing this for?
preview.next: What's the business called?

templates.title: Electrical quote
templates.description: Get enough detail on an electrical job to price it or plan a visit.
templates.metaDescription: Collect electrical job requests with the work type, property, access and photos. Anyone reporting sparks, burning or a shock is told to get urgent help instead.
templates.blurb: Written for electricians and small contracting firms. The first question checks for danger, and anyone describing sparks, burning or a shock is sent straight to urgent advice instead of a quote queue. Faults get asked how far the problem spreads; new work gets asked what and how much, and everyone is asked for photos of the fuse board.

preview.greeting: Need an electrician? Tell us about the job and we'll come back with a price or a time to look.
preview.question: First, a safety check: is anything sparking, smelling of burning, or has anyone had a shock?
preview.next: What kind of work is it?

templates.title: Freelance quote
templates.description: Everything a freelancer needs to price a project before the first call.
templates.metaDescription: A quote form for freelancers: deliverables, where the work will be used, who signs it off, deadline and budget. Committee sign-offs name who has the final say.
templates.blurb: For designers, writers, developers and other freelancers who quote project by project. It asks the things that quietly change a price, such as where the work will be used, whether the deadline is fixed and how many people sign it off, and when a client wants changes to something that already exists, it asks to see it. Work signed off by a committee also asks who settles disagreements, which is where revision rounds multiply.

preview.greeting: Hi! Tell me about your project and I'll send you a quote.
preview.question: What's your name?
preview.next: And the best email for the quote?

templates.title: Graphic design quote
templates.description: Scope a design job, from one flyer to a full identity, before quoting.
templates.metaDescription: Quote design work with the pieces, sizes, brand files, copy and print details up front. Clients with no brand yet get asked about the look they want instead.
templates.blurb: For graphic designers and small studios. Clients with a brand are asked to upload it; clients without one are asked what feel they're after, so you know whether you're designing a flyer or a whole identity. Anything going to print is asked for sizes and quantities, which is where design quotes most often go wrong.

preview.greeting: Looking for a designer? Tell me what you need and I'll put a quote together.
preview.question: Who am I talking to?
preview.next: What's the business or project called?

templates.title: Plumbing quote
templates.description: Understand a plumbing job before you quote it or book a visit.
templates.metaDescription: Take plumbing job requests with the problem, property, photos and access in one chat. Active leaks get told to shut off the water and call, not wait for a quote.
templates.blurb: For plumbers and small plumbing firms. It opens with how urgent the job is, and anyone with water leaking right now is told to turn off the stopcock and call instead of joining the queue. Installations are asked who supplies the fittings, which is the question that most often changes the price.

preview.greeting: Plumbing problem or a new job? Tell us about it and we'll come back with a price.
preview.question: How urgent is it?
preview.answer: Water is leaking or flooding right now

templates.title: Translation quote

templates.metaDescription: Price translation work from the language pair, word count, subject, file format and deadline. Documents for an official body get asked about certification.
templates.blurb: For freelance translators and small agencies. It asks the details that set the rate: the language pair, the subject, the word count and whether the files are editable or scanned. Anything going to a court, embassy or government office is asked what kind of certified translation it needs, so nobody finds out too late.

preview.greeting: Need something translated? Tell us about it and we'll send you a quote.

templates.metaDescription: A quote request form that asks what the price depends on: new builds, redesigns and ongoing support each get their own questions, then budget and deadline.
templates.blurb: Most quote forms collect a name and a vague description, then cost you a discovery call anyway. preview.greeting: Tell us what you need and we'll come back with a price.
preview.question: What's your name?

preview.question: Let's start with your details
preview.next: Which class would you like to join?

preview.question: First, your details

templates.blurb: Journalists get a short, clear route to your press team instead of a generic inbox. The form asks what kind of request it is and follows up to match: preferred format and spokesperson for an interview, which assets for a media kit request, and location details for filming.

templates.blurb: Everything IT needs to set someone up before their first morning: start date, role, systems and equipment. templates.blurb: Asks what the person needs, what it is for and how they want to receive it. preview.greeting: Looking for some information from us? Tell us what you need and we'll get it to you.

templates.title: Logo design brief

templates.blurb: Written from the designer's side of the table: what the business does, who it serves, the personality it wants and every place the logo has to work. preview.greeting: Let's start on your logo. The more you tell us here, the closer the first drafts will be.

templates.blurb: After a one-line summary and the details, it asks whether something is broken, needs changing or is new, and anyone reporting a fault is asked when it started and whether there's a workaround. Changes to existing systems name the system, and only requests with a real deadline are asked for the date and what it depends on.

preview.greeting: Have something you'd like built or changed? Start with the problem and we'll work out the solution together.
preview.question: Who is making the request?

templates.blurb: People ask for solutions; roadmaps need problems. templates.metaDescription: Sign people up to your program, club or community in about two minutes. Group signups get two questions of their own, and everyone hears what comes next.
templates.blurb: Most signup forms stop at a name and an email, and you learn nothing you can act on. This one also asks what people want from joining and how they like to hear from you. preview.greeting: Want early access? Tell us a little about how you'd use it.
preview.question: What email should the invite go to?

templates.blurb: An email address alone gives you a number to announce and nothing to act on. The form also asks why someone came: customers, people still deciding and readers who are here for the writing each get one follow-up of their own.

preview.greeting: Want the newsletter? Tell us what to send and how often.

preview.next: First name, so we're not writing to a stranger?

templates.title: Gym member satisfaction
templates.description: Rate the equipment, classes and staff, and catch members who are close to cancelling.
templates.metaDescription: Ask gym members about equipment, classes, staff and crowding, then find out who is thinking of cancelling and what would keep them training with you.
templates.blurb: Covers what members actually use, a quick grid on the things that make or break a gym, and a ranked wishlist. Members who admit they have thought about cancelling get two extra questions about why and what would keep them, plus the option to have the manager get in touch.

preview.greeting: Hi! We'd love to hear how training with us is going. It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: How long have you been a member?

templates.title: Price sensitivity
templates.description: Four price-point questions in the Van Westendorp style, with value and context around them.
templates.metaDescription: Find the price range customers will accept with four price-point questions, plus what they value, how they'd react to a rise and how they prefer to pay.
templates.blurb: Built around the four classic price-point questions, asked in a fixed order from most expensive to least, so everyone works down the same ladder. Current customers first say what justifies the cost, former customers say why they stopped, and prospects go straight to the price questions.

preview.greeting: Hi! We're working out our pricing and want your honest view. It takes about four minutes.
preview.question: Which of these describes you?

templates.title: Restaurant visit survey
templates.description: Learn who your diners are, how each visit rated and what they want from the menu.
templates.metaDescription: Survey diners on how often they come, how they found you, food, service and prices, what drives their choice of restaurant, and what to add to the menu.
templates.blurb: A survey for planning, not just complaint handling: it learns how often each diner comes, asks first-timers how they found you, and rates food, service and prices. A low overall rating opens questions on exactly which parts let the diner down, and everyone ranks what matters when they choose where to eat.

preview.greeting: Thanks for eating with us! We're planning the next few months and would love your view. It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: What was your most recent visit for?

templates.title: System usability
templates.description: A task check, ten standard usability statements and the moments people got stuck.
templates.metaDescription: Ask users about a task they just finished, rate ten standard usability statements, and find where they slowed down, with a follow-up for anyone who got stuck.
templates.blurb: Anchored to a real task: people say what they tried to do and whether they managed it, and anyone who didn't is asked where they got stuck. The ten standard usability statements sit in one grid, so you can score them the usual way, and willing users can sign up for a follow-up session.

preview.greeting: Thanks for trying the system. A few questions about how that went, about four minutes.
preview.question: What were you trying to do just now?
preview.next: Did you manage to do it?

templates.title: Website questionnaire
templates.description: Find out what visitors came for, and where the site let them down.
templates.metaDescription: Ask visitors why they came to your website, whether they found it, and where they got stuck. People who came up empty are asked what they were looking for.
templates.blurb: Built around the visit someone just had, not their opinion of your brand. It asks what they came to do and whether they managed it: a visitor who found it easily moves straight on, one who had to dig is asked where, and one who gave up is asked what was missing and where they looked.

preview.greeting: Hi! Got a minute to tell us how your visit to our website went?
preview.question: What brought you to the site today?

templates.title: Customer effort score (CES)
templates.description: One effort question, and a closer look at the steps that made it hard.
templates.metaDescription: Measure how easy one task felt with a customer effort score question, then ask customers who struggled exactly which step made it harder than it should be.
templates.blurb: Asks the standard effort question about one named task, on a seven-point agree scale. Customers who found it hard are asked what got in the way, how many times they had to get in touch and which step they would remove; customers who found it easy just say what helped.

preview.greeting: Quick one about what you just did with us. It takes under a minute.
preview.question: What were you trying to do?

templates.title: Customer service satisfaction
templates.description: Rate the help, then check whether the problem is actually solved.
templates.metaDescription: Rate a support conversation on clarity, courtesy and speed, then check if the issue is truly fixed. Open cases get a reopen option instead of a thank-you.
templates.blurb: Keeps the person who helped separate from the outcome, because a friendly agent can still leave a problem open. Customers whose issue is fully sorted are asked what the agent did well; anyone with a partly or fully open case can ask to have it reopened and leave an email, and lands on an ending that says so.

preview.greeting: Thanks for getting in touch with us recently. How did we do?
preview.question: How did you get in touch?

templates.title: Restaurant satisfaction survey
templates.description: Diners rate food, service and value, and unhappy guests reach the manager.
templates.metaDescription: Ask diners about the food, the service and the value of their visit. Dine-in and takeaway guests get different questions, and unhappy ones can ask for the manager.
templates.blurb: Asks guests who ate in about the room and the service, and takeaway or delivery customers whether their order arrived complete. Everyone rates the food and value; a low overall score asks what would have made it better and offers a call from the manager, while happy diners are asked what they enjoyed.

preview.greeting: Thanks for eating with us! Can we ask how it went?
preview.question: When did you eat with us?
preview.next: How did you have your meal?

templates.title: Student satisfaction survey
templates.description: Teaching, resources, workload and support, from the students themselves.
templates.metaDescription: Ask students about teaching, feedback, workload and support services. Students who are struggling can ask to be contacted by support; everyone else stays anonymous.
templates.blurb: Covers the parts of a course students feel most: teaching, feedback on their work, resources, workload and belonging. A student who rates their course low is asked what's making it hard and can ask student support to get in touch, while everyone else can answer without giving a name.

preview.greeting: Hi! We'd like to hear how your course is going. It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: Which course or programme are you studying?
preview.next: Which year are you in?

templates.title: Salon evaluation survey
templates.description: Hear how the appointment went, from consultation to the final look.
templates.metaDescription: Ask salon clients about the consultation, comfort, timing and whether the result matched what they asked for. A result that missed offers a follow-up call.
templates.blurb: Follows a visit in the order it happened: what they had done, the consultation, comfort and timing, then the result itself. A client who says the result wasn't what they wanted is asked what was different and whether they'd like a call about putting it right, before they tell anyone else.

preview.greeting: Thanks for visiting us! How did your appointment go?
preview.question: What did you have done?

templates.title: Event satisfaction survey
templates.description: What worked, what disappointed, and whether people will come back.
templates.metaDescription: Collect attendee feedback after your event: sessions, venue or stream quality, and what disappointed them. In-person and online guests get their own questions.
templates.blurb: Splits in-person and online attendees early, so one group rates the venue and check-in and the other rates the stream. Attendees who found it better than expected are asked for the highlight, while those who found it worse are asked what fell short, before everyone ranks what they value.

preview.greeting: Thanks for coming! A few quick questions while the event is fresh.
preview.question: How did you attend?

templates.title: Resident satisfaction survey
templates.description: Housing and community services, rated by the people who live there.
templates.metaDescription: Ask residents about repairs, shared spaces, safety and communication. Repairs that are still open get their own follow-up, and residents can ask to be contacted.
templates.blurb: Covers the services residents notice day to day, from repairs and cleaning to safety and how well they are kept informed. Anyone with a repair that was botched or is still waiting is asked exactly what and where, and residents who want a reply can leave details and land on an ending that says someone will be in touch.

preview.greeting: Hello! We'd like to know how living here is going for you. It takes about four minutes.
preview.question: Which building or street do you live in?
preview.next: How long have you lived here?

templates.title: Member satisfaction survey
templates.description: Find out what members value, and why some might not renew.
templates.metaDescription: Learn which membership benefits people value, how they take part and whether they plan to renew. Members thinking of leaving are asked why and what would keep them.
templates.blurb: Asks why people joined, ranks the benefits they care about and checks whether you contact them too much or too little. The renewal question decides the rest: loyal members say what they value most, undecided ones say what would help them choose, and members leaning towards leaving are asked why and what would change their mind.

preview.greeting: Hi! As a member, your view shapes what we do next. This takes about three minutes.
preview.question: How long have you been a member?

templates.title: Customer satisfaction (CSAT)
templates.description: Rate a specific interaction, and dig only where it went badly.
templates.metaDescription: A short CSAT survey about one interaction. Customers with nothing left open finish in a few taps; the rest say what's outstanding and can ask for a follow-up.
templates.blurb: CSAT works when it is asked about one thing, straight after that thing happened. A customer with nothing outstanding gives one reason for their score and is done; anyone left with something unsorted is asked what is outstanding and what got in the way, and can ask a person to pick it up. Nobody is asked what went wrong when nothing did.

preview.greeting: How did that go? A couple of questions while it's fresh.
preview.question: What are you rating today?

templates.title: NPS survey
templates.description: Measure loyalty, then ask detractors, passives and promoters different things.
templates.metaDescription: A Net Promoter Score survey that asks detractors, passives and promoters different follow-ups, so every score arrives with a reason your team can act on.
templates.blurb: The score on its own tells you almost nothing you can act on, and one follow-up cannot serve every part of the scale. A 3 is asked what went wrong and whether they are thinking of leaving, a 7 is asked what would make it a 9, and a 10 is asked what to quote, so one survey produces a fix list, a wish list and a testimonial list.

preview.greeting: One quick question, plus a follow-up. It takes about a minute.
preview.question: How likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague?
preview.next: What would it take for you to give us a 9 or a 10?

templates.title: Customer development
templates.description: Understand a problem through people's real behaviour, before you build anything.
templates.metaDescription: Learn how people handle a problem today before you pitch a fix. Asks about the last time it happened, their workarounds, time lost and whether they would talk.
templates.blurb: Built around what people have actually done, not what they say they would buy. It asks about the last time the problem came up, what they use now and how many hours it eats, then screens out anyone who never faces it. Only people who have tried to fix it are asked what failed, and anyone willing to talk is asked for an email.

preview.greeting: We're trying to understand how people plan staff shifts today. No sales pitch, just a few questions.
preview.question: Which of these describes you best?
preview.answer: I own or run the business

templates.title: Customer loyalty
templates.description: Learn what keeps customers coming back and what could pull them away.
templates.metaDescription: Find out why customers stay, what would make them switch and whether they're shopping around. Customers wavering on a return get their own follow-up question.
templates.blurb: Satisfied customers still leave, so this survey asks about the relationship rather than one visit: why people come back, how much they trust you and what would make them switch. Anyone unlikely to return is asked why straight away instead of being asked what keeps them, and only customers who have looked at alternatives are asked what they found.

preview.greeting: You've stuck with us, and we'd love to know why. A few quick questions.
preview.question: How long have you been a customer?

templates.title: Customer needs
templates.description: Find out what customers are trying to achieve and what stands in their way.
templates.metaDescription: Ask customers what they're trying to get done, what gets in the way and which improvements matter most. People who feel poorly served get asked what's missing.
templates.blurb: Starts from the customer's goal instead of your feature list, then asks what slows them down, how much each quality matters and which improvements they would rank first. Customers who say current options only partly work, or not at all, are asked what's missing before anything else.

preview.greeting: Help us understand what you need from us. It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: What are you trying to get done when you come to us?
preview.next: How often do you need to do that?

templates.title: Help desk feedback
templates.description: Check whether a help desk request was understood, explained and actually fixed.
templates.metaDescription: Ask users whether the help desk understood their request, explained the fix clearly and got them working again. Unresolved tickets get a chance to reopen.
templates.blurb: Sent after a ticket closes, it asks the question most help desk surveys skip: is the problem really fixed? Anyone who says no is asked what still isn't working and whether to reopen the ticket, before rating how well the request was understood and explained.

preview.greeting: Your help desk request was closed. Mind telling us how it went? It takes a minute.
preview.question: What was the ticket number, if you have it?
preview.next: What did you contact us about?

templates.title: Hotel guest feedback
templates.description: Hear how a stay really went, from check-in to anything that went wrong.
templates.metaDescription: Ask guests about the room, the staff, the facilities and anything that went wrong. Guests who want a reply are routed to the manager with their email.
templates.blurb: Covers each part of a stay in one grid, then asks the question that matters most to a hotel manager: did anything go wrong, and did the team fix it? Guests with no problems skip straight past it, and anyone who wants the manager to reply leaves an email and gets a different sign-off.

preview.greeting: Thanks for staying with us. How was it? A few questions, about two minutes.
preview.question: When did you check out?
preview.next: What brought you here?

templates.title: Service evaluation
templates.description: Evaluate a service against the job it was hired to do.
templates.metaDescription: Judge a service against the job it was meant to do. Rates delivery, quality and usefulness, then asks what went well or where it went wrong, based on the answer.
templates.blurb: Asks what the client needed the service to do before asking how it went, so every rating has something to be measured against. If the service did the job, it asks which step worked best; if it only partly did, it asks where things went wrong and how much that mattered.

preview.greeting: We'd like to know how well our service did its job for you. About two minutes.
preview.question: Which service are you evaluating?
preview.next: What did you need this service to do for you?

templates.title: Software satisfaction
templates.description: Measure how users feel about your software, and catch bugs and gaps along the way.
templates.metaDescription: Ask users how satisfied they are with your software, which parts work well, what's missing and whether bugs got in the way. Unhappy users say why first.
templates.blurb: Built for software teams: a satisfaction score, a grid for ease of use, speed, features, docs and support, and a ranking of what users value most. Unhappy users are asked why before anything else, and only people who hit a bug are asked to describe it and attach a screenshot.

preview.greeting: Help us make the software better for you. About three minutes.
preview.question: How long have you been using our software?

templates.title: Company satisfaction
templates.description: Learn how people feel about working here, and who might be thinking of leaving.
templates.metaDescription: Ask employees how they feel about their work, manager, pay, workload and leadership. Unhappy staff are asked if they've thought about leaving, and why.
templates.blurb: Covers the whole job in one grid, from day-to-day work to pay and leadership, then asks people to rank the changes that would matter most. Staff who wouldn't recommend working here are asked whether they have thought about leaving and what is behind it, while happier staff are asked what's worth protecting.

preview.greeting: This survey is anonymous and takes about four minutes. Honest answers help most.
preview.question: Which part of the company do you work in?

templates.title: New hire onboarding
templates.description: Find out whether new starters got what they needed in their first weeks.
templates.metaDescription: Ask new hires whether their equipment was ready, who they met and what still feels unclear. Anyone with open questions can ask HR to get in touch.
templates.blurb: Asks the practical questions first: was the laptop ready, did the logins work, who introduced themselves. Then it checks whether the new hire knows what's expected of them. Anyone still unsure is asked what about, and can leave their details for HR to follow up.

preview.greeting: Welcome aboard! Tell us how your first few weeks have gone. About three minutes.
preview.question: How long ago did you start?

templates.title: IT satisfaction
templates.description: Find out how well everyday tech and IT support are working for your team.
templates.metaDescription: Ask staff how well their laptops, Wi-Fi, apps and IT support work for them, how often tech gets in the way and what would help. Only help desk users rate support.
templates.blurb: Rates each everyday system in one grid, from laptops to video calls, and asks how often tech problems interrupt real work. Only people who have asked IT for help recently are asked to rate the support, so the scores come from people who have actually used it.

preview.greeting: How well is your tech working for you? A few quick questions for the IT team.
preview.question: Where do you mostly work?

templates.title: Engagement pulse
templates.description: A short, repeatable check that follows up with the people who are struggling.
templates.metaDescription: A short anonymous pulse survey to send monthly: five statements, an eNPS score and a follow-up asking anyone who is struggling what's weighing on them.
templates.blurb: Short enough to send every month and consistent enough to trend: five statements on workload, clarity, support, growth and belonging, plus an eNPS score. Anyone who scores 6 or below is asked what's weighing on them and what would help this month, which is where the comments worth reading come from.

preview.greeting: Quick pulse check. Anonymous, and under two minutes.
preview.question: Which team are you in?

templates.title: Manager effectiveness
templates.description: Hear from a team how their manager really supports them, one behaviour at a time.
templates.metaDescription: Ask direct reports how their manager handles priorities, feedback, decisions and growth. Low scores lead to one concrete change; high scores to what to keep.
templates.blurb: Rates the specific things a manager does, such as setting priorities, giving feedback and making timely decisions, instead of asking for one vague grade. People who score their manager low are asked for the single change that would help most and can request a private follow-up, while those who score high are asked what the manager should keep doing.

preview.greeting: This is a few minutes of honest feedback about your manager. Answer for how things usually are, not your best or worst week.
preview.question: Which manager is this feedback about?
preview.next: How long have you reported to this manager?

templates.title: Pre-event survey
templates.description: Find out what registered attendees want and need before the doors open.
templates.metaDescription: Ask registered attendees what they hope to get out of the event, which sessions they want, and what they need to take part, from dietary to access needs.
templates.blurb: Sent after registration, it asks what people want to learn, which sessions they care about and how much they already know, so speakers can pitch their talks at the right level. Only people who say they have access needs are asked for the details, and first-timers get one extra question about what would help them settle in.

preview.greeting: You're registered, thank you! A few quick questions now help us shape the day around the people actually coming.
preview.question: What's your name?
preview.next: Which parts of the event are you planning to attend?

templates.title: Event evaluation
templates.description: Judge an event by whether it did its job for each group who came.
templates.metaDescription: Evaluate an event against why people came: goals met, program, organisation and value. Sponsors and exhibitors get their own questions about leads and traffic.
templates.blurb: Starts by asking why each person came and whether the event delivered it, so the scores you read later have a reason attached. Sponsors and exhibitors are routed to questions about booth traffic and lead quality, and anyone whose goal wasn't met is asked what got in the way before rating the program and organisation.

preview.greeting: Thanks for being part of the event. We'd like an honest look back to plan the next one well.
preview.question: How were you involved?

templates.title: Event questionnaire
templates.description: Collect the purpose, audience and practical needs of an event before anything is booked.
templates.metaDescription: Gather everything needed to shape an event: purpose, audience, format, dates, guest numbers and support needed. Online events skip the venue questions.
templates.blurb: Written for the person commissioning an event, whether that's a client, a manager or a committee, so planning starts from their goals rather than a venue. It asks what success looks like before it asks about logistics. Online events skip straight past the location and venue questions, and hybrid events are asked what remote guests should be able to do before the venue questions.

preview.greeting: Let's pin down what this event needs to be. Answer what you know; rough guesses are fine.
preview.question: Who should we talk to about this event?
preview.next: Which organisation or team is the event for?

templates.title: Event planning survey
templates.description: Ask the people you want in the room what would get them there, before you book anything.
templates.metaDescription: Ask potential attendees which topics, format, timing and cost would get them to come before you book anything. Unlikely attendees are asked what stops them.
templates.blurb: Goes to the audience you hope to attract, not the people already signed up, and asks about topics, format, day, length and what they weigh up when deciding. Anyone who says they're unlikely to come is asked what's stopping them, and people who want first word on dates can leave an email.

preview.greeting: We're planning an event and want to build it around what you'd actually come to. This takes about two minutes.
preview.question: Which best describes you?

templates.title: Post-event feedback
templates.description: Rate the parts of an event separately, and dig in where the score was low.
templates.metaDescription: Rate speakers, venue, food and organisation separately. Low scores ask what let the day down; high scores ask for a highlight and whether they'd speak next time.
templates.blurb: A single "how was it?" averages a great speaker and a cold room into a middling score. The grid shows which one to fix, and anyone who rates the day three stars or fewer is asked what went wrong and whether they want someone to follow up, while people who loved it are asked for a highlight and whether they'd speak at the next one.

preview.greeting: Thanks for coming! A few quick questions on how it went.
preview.question: How would you rate each part?
preview.next: And the event as a whole?

templates.title: Professional development feedback
templates.description: Check whether development support is useful, and what people need to put new skills to work.
templates.metaDescription: Find out whether training, mentoring and learning time actually help your people grow, what gets in the way, and which support they want more of next year.
templates.blurb: Built for an annual or half-year review of your learning programme. The usefulness score decides the follow-up: people who got value are asked what helped most, and people who didn't are asked what got in the way. Anyone who took part in nothing skips the usefulness questions and goes straight to what held them back. It ends by asking who wants a conversation about their own development plan, and only those people are asked for an email.

preview.greeting: We want to spend next year's development time and budget where it helps you most. Five minutes?
preview.question: Which best describes your role?

templates.title: Mobile app survey
templates.description: Learn how people use your app, where it frustrates them and what would make it more useful.
templates.metaDescription: Ask users what they open your app to do, how easy it is, what breaks and what they'd change. Problems get a follow-up, and keen users can join your beta list.
templates.blurb: Starts with the one job people open the app for, then asks how easy that job is. Anyone who struggles is asked where they get stuck, and anyone who reports crashes or slowness describes the last time it happened, which is what your developers need. Users who want to test new features leave an email and get their own ending.

preview.greeting: Hi! A few quick questions about the app. Your answers go straight to the people who build it.
preview.question: Which phone do you use the app on?

templates.title: Course feedback
templates.description: Hear how students found the content, teaching and workload, and what would help them learn.
templates.metaDescription: An end-of-course survey for students: content, teaching, workload and the support that would have helped. Low scores get a follow-up about what went wrong.
templates.blurb: Covers the things you can actually change before the next run: clarity, pace, materials, assessment and workload in hours rather than adjectives. Students who rate the course low are asked what made it hard, students who rate it well are asked what helped, and everyone says what support would have made the material easier to understand.

preview.greeting: Thanks for taking the course. Your feedback shapes how it runs next time, and it takes about four minutes.
preview.question: Which course are you giving feedback on?
preview.next: How much do you agree with each of these?

templates.title: Sponsorship satisfaction
templates.description: Review the value sponsors received, and find out who is ready to renew.
templates.metaDescription: Ask sponsors what they got from your event or programme: delivery of each benefit, audience fit, communication, and whether they would sign on again next time.
templates.blurb: Asks sponsors to score each benefit you promised, from logo placement to attendee data, so you see what was delivered rather than a vague satisfaction score. Sponsors who got what they came for describe the highlight, the rest explain what fell short, and anyone ready to sponsor again lands on an ending that tells them you'll reach out first.

preview.greeting: Thank you for sponsoring. We'd like to know what worked for you and what we should do better next time.
preview.question: Which company are you answering for?
preview.next: Which sponsorship level did you have?

templates.title: Volunteer feedback
templates.description: Find out how volunteers experienced the day and what would make them come back.
templates.metaDescription: Ask volunteers how prepared, supported and valued they felt, what made the day hard, and what would bring them back. Bad experiences get a coordinator follow-up.
templates.blurb: Checks the basics that decide whether a volunteer returns: did they know their role, have what they needed, know who to ask and feel their time was valued. Someone who had a rough day is asked what went wrong and whether the coordinator can get in touch, and only people who say yes leave their details, so everyone else stays anonymous. Everyone says what would make it easier to help again.

preview.greeting: Thank you for giving your time. Could you tell us how it went? It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: Which activity or event did you volunteer at?
preview.next: Was this your first time volunteering with us?

templates.title: Brand awareness survey
templates.description: Find out who remembers your brand unprompted, who recognises it, and where they came across it.
templates.metaDescription: Measure unaided recall before naming your brand, then recognition, where people saw you and what they think. People who don't know you skip straight past it.
templates.blurb: Asks the unprompted question first, before your brand name appears anywhere, so recall is real. Only people who recognise the brand are asked where they saw it, whether they've bought it and how it comes across, while everyone else skips ahead to what drives their choices. Written for a coffee brand as an example, so swap in your own category and names.

preview.greeting: Hi! We're asking people about the brands they buy. There are no right answers, and it takes about three minutes.
preview.question: How often do you buy coffee to make at home?

templates.title: Management survey
templates.description: Hear how priorities, decisions, communication and support feel from inside the team.
templates.metaDescription: Ask teams how work is managed: clear priorities, how decisions are made and shared, manager support and what slows them down. Anonymous and quick to answer.
templates.blurb: Separates the parts of management people usually lump together: whether priorities are clear and stable, who actually makes decisions, whether work is shared fairly and how much their own manager helps. People who rate their manager's support low pick what's missing, and people who rate it high name the habit worth spreading. It closes by asking how confident they are that anything will change.

preview.greeting: This survey is anonymous. We want to know how work is managed here, honestly, so we can fix what isn't working.
preview.question: Which area do you work in?

templates.title: Post-training survey
templates.description: Find out what learners can actually use after training, and what might stop them.
templates.metaDescription: After a training session, ask what people understood, how their confidence changed, what they'll try first and what could get in the way of using it at work.
templates.blurb: Goes past 'did you enjoy it' to whether the training will change anything: a before-and-after confidence check, the first thing each person plans to try, and the obstacles they expect. Anyone who says little of it applies to their job explains why, and people who want a check-in a month later leave an email and get their own ending.

preview.greeting: Thanks for joining the training. A few questions about what you'll take back to work, about three minutes.
preview.question: Which training did you attend?
preview.next: How did you take it?

templates.title: Exit interview
templates.description: Ask why someone is leaving in a way they can answer honestly.
templates.metaDescription: Ask departing employees why they're leaving in a way they can answer honestly. The follow-up matches their main reason, from pay and growth to their manager.
templates.blurb: Leaving is when people say what they meant. Structured enough to count across a year of departures, open enough to catch what no option covers, and the follow-up matches the reason, so someone leaving over their manager is not asked about salary bands. It ends with whether they'd come back, which is worth knowing.

preview.greeting: Before you go: your honest answers help the people who are staying. This is confidential.
preview.question: How long have you worked here?

templates.title: Product feedback
templates.description: Learn what users rely on, what gets in their way and what they want next.
templates.metaDescription: Ask users what they use your product for, where it gets in the way and what to build next. Low scores get asked about the obstacle, high scores about what works.
templates.blurb: Starts with the job people hire your product for, then rates it on the things that matter. The overall score decides the next question: happy users are asked what they would hate to lose, and unhappy ones describe the last time it got in their way and whether it blocks them outright.

preview.greeting: Thanks for using the product. Five minutes of your honest opinion will shape what we build next.
preview.question: In a sentence, what do you mainly use it for?
preview.next: How often do you use it?

templates.title: Branding questionnaire
templates.description: Everything a designer needs to know about a business before brand work starts.
templates.metaDescription: A brand discovery questionnaire for designers and agencies: business, audience, personality, competitors and deliverables. Rebrands also get asked what to keep.
templates.blurb: Covers the business, the customer, the personality and the practical scope, so the first meeting starts from answers instead of a blank page. Clients refreshing an existing brand are asked what works now, what doesn't and to upload their current files. A brand new business skips straight to its audience.

preview.greeting: Before we start on your brand, we'd like to understand the business behind it. This takes about ten minutes.
preview.question: First, who are we working with?
preview.next: What's the name of the business?

templates.title: Cancellation survey
templates.description: Find out why people leave, and ask each of them the one follow-up that fits.
templates.metaDescription: Find out why customers cancel a subscription or service. The reason they pick decides the one follow-up worth asking, and nobody is pushed to stay.
templates.blurb: The exit is the most honest moment you get, and the reason decides what is worth asking next. Price gets a question about what would have felt fair, a missing feature gets asked which one, and a switch to a competitor gets asked what they do better. "No longer need it" is left alone. Nobody is talked out of leaving.

preview.greeting: Sorry to see you go. A couple of quick questions, and then you're done. Your cancellation goes ahead either way.
preview.question: What's the main reason you're cancelling?

templates.title: Customer success story
templates.description: Collect a customer's story in their own words, ready to shape into a case study.
templates.metaDescription: Gather material for a case study: the problem, why they chose you, how they use it and the results, and permission to publish with their name or anonymously.
templates.blurb: Walks a customer through the story in the order a case study is written: before, the decision, the day to day and the results. Anyone with a figure to share is asked how they measured it. Customers who agree to be named are asked for a headshot, and those who prefer to stay anonymous are asked how they'd like to be described.

preview.greeting: Thanks for agreeing to share your story. Answer in your own words; we'll do the tidying up and show you the draft before anything goes out.
preview.question: Let's start with your details.
preview.next: Which company do you work for?

templates.title: Email design brief
templates.description: Collect the audience, message, action and practical limits before designing an email.
templates.metaDescription: Brief an email designer properly: the type of email, audience, main action, copy, brand files, sending platform and deadline. Series and brand files get follow-ups.
templates.blurb: Asks what a designer needs before opening a layout tool: who the email is for, the one action it should drive, who writes the copy and what it must work with. Clients ordering a series are asked how many emails, and anyone with brand guidelines is asked to upload them.

preview.greeting: Let's plan your email. A few questions now saves a round of revisions later.
preview.question: Who should we send the designs to?
preview.next: Which company or brand is this for?

templates.title: Lead generation survey
templates.description: Learn what potential buyers need, then invite the ones who want help to talk.
templates.metaDescription: A lead generation survey that asks about needs first and contact details last. People who want a call get their own path; others can leave without sharing an email.
templates.blurb: Asks about the problem, what has been tried and how urgent it is before asking for any details, so people answer as themselves rather than as a lead. At the end they choose what they want from you: a call, a written summary, or nothing at all. Each choice gets its own path and its own sign-off.

preview.greeting: We're learning how teams like yours handle this problem. A few quick questions, and you decide at the end whether we follow up.
preview.question: Which best describes your role?

templates.title: SaaS onboarding survey
templates.description: Find out whether new users reached their first goal, and where setup stopped them.
templates.metaDescription: Ask new users what they signed up to do, whether they got there and where setup got hard. Stuck users get their own follow-up and can ask for a walkthrough.
templates.blurb: Built around the first thing a new user wanted to get done. People who got there easily move on quickly, people who struggled say which part took effort, and people who are still stuck name the step and describe it. Anyone can ask for a walkthrough at the end, and those who do get their own ending.

preview.greeting: Welcome aboard. Tell us how your first few days went, so we can make them easier for you and everyone after you.
preview.question: When you signed up, what were you hoping to get done first?
preview.next: How are you using it?

templates.title: Client satisfaction
templates.description: Check in with ongoing clients on results, communication and whether they plan to stay.
templates.metaDescription: A client satisfaction survey for ongoing clients: results, communication and value. Clients unsure about renewing are offered a call before they decide.
templates.blurb: Made for a regular check-in with retained clients rather than a one-off project debrief. Clients whose results fell short are asked where and what would put it right, and the rest are asked what they'd hate to lose. Anyone unsure about continuing is offered a call from their account lead, and those who accept get their own ending.

preview.greeting: Thanks for working with us. We'd like to know how things are really going. This takes about three minutes.
preview.question: Which service or account are you answering about?
preview.next: Overall, how satisfied are you with working with us?

templates.title: Internal communication survey
templates.description: Find out where information flows well at work, and where it gets lost.
templates.metaDescription: An internal communication survey for employees: clarity of goals, access to information, useful channels, handoffs and whether people feel able to raise concerns.
templates.blurb: Asks employees whether they understand the goals, can find what they need and hear about changes in time, then has them rank the channels they actually rely on. Anyone who says they would keep a concern to themselves is asked what would make speaking up easier, a question most surveys never reach.

preview.greeting: This survey is about how information moves around here. There are no right answers, and honest ones help most.
preview.question: Which part of the organisation do you work in?

templates.title: Employee benefits survey
templates.description: Learn which benefits people know about, use and value, and which ones they can't reach.
templates.metaDescription: Find out which benefits employees know about, use and value, where access breaks down and what is missing. Low scores and failed claims get their own follow-up.
templates.blurb: Separates the three reasons a benefit fails: nobody knows it exists, nobody values it, or it is too hard to use. A low satisfaction score gets a question about why, and anyone who gave up on using a benefit is asked which one and what got in the way. It ends with a ranking of where to invest next.

preview.greeting: We're reviewing our benefits and want to spend on what matters to you. Your answers are anonymous and take about five minutes.
preview.question: How long have you worked here?

templates.title: Healthcare staff satisfaction
templates.description: Understand how healthcare staff experience their work, without collecting patient details.
templates.metaDescription: An anonymous survey for clinical and support staff on workload, staffing, equipment, breaks, burnout and whether they plan to stay. No patient details collected.
templates.blurb: Written for wards, clinics and practices, where satisfaction depends on staffing, handovers, breaks and feeling safe to speak up. Staff who say they often feel burned out are asked what drives it, and anyone unsure about staying is asked what would keep them. Open questions remind people to leave patient details out.

preview.greeting: This survey is anonymous and takes about five minutes. Please don't include patient names or details in any answer.
preview.question: Which best describes your role?

templates.title: Competitor research
templates.description: Find out who you were compared with, on what, and why the buyer went the way they did.
templates.metaDescription: Ask recent buyers which alternatives they compared, what mattered most and why they chose who they did. Won, lost and undecided buyers each get their own follow-up.
templates.blurb: Built for buyers who have just made a decision, including the ones who went elsewhere. It maps the shortlist and the criteria first, then asks one question that splits the path: buyers who chose you say what tipped it, buyers who chose a rival say what made that option the better fit, and anyone still deciding says what is holding them up.

preview.greeting: You recently looked at a few options, us among them. Mind telling us how that comparison went? Honest answers help most.
preview.question: What was your part in the decision?

templates.title: Working style questionnaire
templates.description: Help people describe how they like to work, in their own words, as a start to a team conversation.
templates.metaDescription: A low-stakes personality questionnaire about working style: energy, focus, feedback and how people handle pressure. Built for team conversations, not for labels.
templates.blurb: Everyday questions about energy, focus, decisions and feedback, and each person picks who can see their answers before they start. Anyone who says pressure tends to overwhelm them is asked what actually helps, so a manager has something to act on.

preview.greeting: A few questions about how you like to work. There are no right answers, and nothing here is a test.
preview.question: What should we call you?
preview.next: Before we start: who would you like to see your answers?

templates.title: Eating habits survey
templates.description: Understand eating patterns, food choices and the practical barriers behind them.
templates.metaDescription: Learn how people really eat: the diet they follow and why, how often they cook, what they snack on and what gets in the way of eating the way they would like to.
templates.blurb: Covers the diet someone follows, a week of typical eating in one grid, what drives their choices and what makes eating well harder. People who follow a particular diet are asked why, and everyone else skips straight past it.

preview.greeting: Hi! This is a short survey about everyday eating habits. Answers are for general research, and nothing here is judged.
preview.question: Do you follow a particular way of eating?

templates.title: Facebook audience survey
templates.description: Learn why people follow your Page or Group and what would get them more involved.
templates.metaDescription: Ask the members of your Facebook Page or Group why they follow, what they want more of and what stops them joining in. Quiet readers get their own follow-up.
templates.blurb: Short enough to finish from a link in a post. It asks how people found you, why they stay and which formats they want, then splits on how they take part: members who comment or post say what got them talking, and quiet readers say what holds them back.

preview.greeting: Thanks for being part of our community on Facebook. We'd love to know what you want from it. It takes about two minutes.
preview.question: How did you first find us on Facebook?
preview.answer: A friend shared or invited me

templates.title: Insurance needs questionnaire
templates.description: Collect needs, current cover and priorities before an insurance review call.
templates.metaDescription: Gather what an adviser needs before an insurance conversation: personal or business cover, current policies, renewal dates and priorities. Urgent cases are flagged.
templates.blurb: Asks personal and business clients different questions, so a family never sees a question about employees. Anyone already insured is asked for their current provider and renewal date, and people who need cover within a week land on their own ending so the team can call them first.

preview.greeting: Hi! A few questions so our adviser understands what you need before you talk. It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: Who is the cover for?

templates.title: Lost customer survey
templates.description: Learn what changed for a customer who stopped buying, and how you compare with where they went.
templates.metaDescription: Ask customers who stopped buying what changed, whether they told you, and how the business they use now compares. Anyone open to a chat can ask for a call.
templates.blurb: For customers who drifted away rather than formally cancelling, such as a client who stopped reordering or a regular who stopped coming in. It asks what changed and whether they ever told you, which shows how many losses you could have seen coming. Price leavers get a pricing question, people who moved elsewhere compare you side by side, and anyone open to a conversation reaches an ending that promises a call.

preview.greeting: We noticed we haven't seen you in a while. Would you tell us what changed? It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: How long were you buying from us?

templates.title: Customer retention survey
templates.description: Ask current customers what keeps them with you and what could change their mind.
templates.metaDescription: Find out why current customers stay, what nearly made them leave and whether they expect to renew. Anyone who came close to leaving gets extra follow-ups.
templates.blurb: Built for customers who are still with you, which is when their answers are most useful. It measures the value they get and why they stay, then asks one direct question: has anything come close to making you leave? Those who say yes are asked what happened and what you should fix first, and everyone says whether they expect to still be a customer a year from now, so at-risk accounts surface before they cancel.

preview.greeting: You've been with us a while, and we'd like to keep earning that. Mind answering a few questions?
preview.question: How long have you been a customer?

templates.title: Fashion shopper questionnaire
templates.description: Understand your fashion customers' style, spending and what persuades them to buy.
templates.metaDescription: Learn how your fashion audience shops: their style, budget, where they buy and what makes them trust a brand. Online and in-store shoppers get their own follow-ups.
templates.blurb: A questionnaire for clothing and accessory brands that want to know their audience beyond age and location. It covers style, budget and what they weigh when buying, and the shopping channel decides the next question: online shoppers are asked what helps them buy without trying on, and in-store shoppers what draws them through the door.

preview.greeting: Hi! We're a fashion brand trying to understand how you like to shop. It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: Which age group are you in?

templates.title: Firmographics survey
templates.description: Profile the companies in your audience by size, sector, model and who makes buying decisions.
templates.metaDescription: Collect company size, industry, location, business model and buying role from B2B respondents, with an optional follow-up for those who want to talk to sales.
templates.blurb: The company facts that give B2B research and sales conversations context: industry, headcount, revenue band, locations and business model. It also asks the respondent's part in buying decisions, skipping the budget question for people who are not involved, and anyone who wants a follow-up leaves their details and gets their own ending.

preview.greeting: Hello! We're learning about the businesses we work with. A few quick questions about your company.
preview.question: Which industry is your company in?

templates.title: Food preferences survey
templates.description: Learn what people like to eat, what they avoid and what they value when choosing food.
templates.metaDescription: Ask about diets, allergies, favourite cuisines and what people value in a meal. Use it to plan a menu, test a food idea or learn what your customers like to eat.
templates.blurb: A food preferences survey for restaurants, caterers and food brands. It starts with diets and allergies, asking for details only from people who have an allergy, then covers cuisines, spice, eating-out habits and what matters most in a meal, finishing with the dish people wish they could find.

preview.greeting: Hungry for a quick chat? We'd love to hear what you like to eat.
preview.question: Do you follow any of these diets?

templates.title: Magazine reader survey
templates.description: Find out which sections readers value, which they skip and what would make them stay.
templates.metaDescription: Ask readers how they read your magazine, which sections they skip and what they want more of. Happy readers name a favourite piece; unhappy ones say what fell flat.
templates.blurb: A reader survey for print and digital magazines. It covers format, reading habits and a section-by-section grid, then splits on the overall rating: readers who love it name the piece that stayed with them, and readers who do not are asked what disappoints them. It closes by asking whether they plan to keep reading.

preview.greeting: Thanks for reading us. We'd like to know what you love, what you skip and what's missing.
preview.question: How do you usually read the magazine?

templates.title: Market segmentation survey
templates.description: Find meaningful groups in your audience based on needs and behaviour.
templates.metaDescription: Group your audience by needs, habits and buying behaviour, not labels alone. Asks about goals, current solutions and attitudes, with background questions last.
templates.blurb: Segments built only on age or job title rarely predict what people buy. This survey asks about needs first: the problem, how often it happens, what people use today and how they choose, with background questions saved for the end. People already using something rate it, and people using nothing are asked why, which often reveals a segment of its own.

preview.greeting: Hi! We're trying to understand the different kinds of people we could help. This takes about four minutes.
preview.question: Rank these goals by how important they are to you right now.
preview.next: How often do you run into the problem you'd most like solved?

templates.title: Media habits survey
templates.description: Learn where your audience gets news and entertainment, and why they choose each channel.
templates.metaDescription: Find out which channels your audience uses for news and entertainment, how often and why. Covers trust, paid subscriptions and how people feel about ads.
templates.blurb: Useful for planning where to advertise, publish or partner. It maps which channels people use and how often, why they turn to media at all and which sources they trust, then asks whether they pay for any subscriptions, with a follow-up only for those who do.

preview.greeting: Hi! We're curious how you keep up with news and entertainment. A few quick questions.
preview.question: How often do you use each of these?
preview.next: On a typical day, how much time do you spend with media of any kind?

templates.title: Meeting feedback
templates.description: Find out whether a meeting was worth it and what would make the next one better.
templates.metaDescription: Ask attendees whether a meeting was worth their time, had a clear purpose and ended with clear next steps. Low scores and unclear actions get their own follow-ups.
templates.blurb: A short check to send right after a meeting. It rates purpose, participation, timekeeping and decisions in one grid, then asks whether it was worth the time: anyone who says no is asked how it could have worked better. Anyone unsure of the next steps is asked what is unclear, so it can be fixed before work stalls.

preview.greeting: Thanks for joining the meeting. Two minutes to help make the next one better?
preview.question: Which meeting are you giving feedback on?
preview.next: What was your part in it?

templates.title: Mystery shopper report
templates.description: Give mystery shoppers a clear, factual way to report each visit.
templates.metaDescription: A structured report for mystery shoppers: visit details, greeting, store condition, staff knowledge, stock and checkout, with photo uploads and factual notes.
templates.blurb: Written for the shopper to fill in straight after a visit, with questions that ask what happened rather than how it felt. In-store visits get a question about the shop's condition that phone and online visits skip, and a missing item prompts a follow-up about what was offered instead. Photos of receipts or displays can be attached as evidence.

preview.greeting: Thanks for completing this visit. Please fill this in as soon as you can, while the details are fresh.
preview.question: Your details
preview.next: Which store or branch did you visit?

templates.title: Newsletter feedback
templates.description: Find out whether your newsletter is useful and what would keep people reading.
templates.metaDescription: Ask subscribers which parts of your newsletter they read, how often they want it and what would improve it. Occasional readers are asked what stops them opening it.
templates.blurb: A short survey to send your subscribers. It asks how they read the newsletter, and the answer decides the next question: engaged readers name their favourite part, while people who open it only now and then, or rarely, are asked what stops them. Everyone then weighs in on frequency, length and topics, and gets a chance to recommend it.

preview.greeting: Hi! You get our newsletter, and we want to make it worth opening. Got a minute?
preview.question: How do you usually read the newsletter?
preview.answer: I read most of every issue

templates.title: Community needs assessment
templates.description: Find out what members need before you plan the next event, channel or program.
templates.metaDescription: Ask members what they joined for, what they want more of and what stops them taking part. Members who offer to help get their own follow-up and sign-off.
templates.blurb: Starts with how long someone has been around and how they take part, so a quiet lurker and a daily poster can be read separately. Members who feel they don't belong are asked what would change that, and anyone who offers to help run something is asked for an email and gets their own thank-you.

preview.greeting: You make this community what it is. Help us decide what to build next? It takes about four minutes.
preview.question: How long have you been part of the community?

templates.title: Path to purchase
templates.description: Map the steps real customers took from first need to final purchase.
templates.metaDescription: Trace how a recent customer went from noticing a need to buying: what triggered it, where they researched, what they compared and what almost stopped them.
templates.blurb: Anchored on one recent purchase, so customers describe what they actually did rather than what they usually do. People who seriously considered a competitor are asked what tipped them your way, and everyone ranks the factors that decided it.

preview.greeting: Thanks for your recent purchase! We'd love to hear how you got here. It's about three minutes.
preview.question: What did you buy from us most recently?
preview.next: What first made you start looking for it?

templates.title: Phone survey script
templates.description: An interviewer script for customer calls that logs outcomes, callbacks and answers.
templates.metaDescription: A phone survey script your callers fill in as they talk: log the call outcome, confirm consent, read each question aloud and record answers in the caller's words.
templates.blurb: Written for the person making the call, with every question worded to be read aloud. The first answer routes the rest: a declined or unanswered call ends straight away, a callback request asks for a time and closes on its own ending, and only a completed call goes on to the questions.

preview.greeting: Interviewer: open this before you dial, and fill it in as the call goes. Read the questions exactly as written.
preview.question: Your name (interviewer)
preview.next: Number called

templates.title: Podcast listener survey
templates.description: Learn who your listeners are, how they listen and what they want next.
templates.metaDescription: Ask listeners how they found the show, when they listen, which formats they enjoy and what topics or guests they want next. Low ratings get their own follow-up.
templates.blurb: Covers the questions podcasters actually argue about: episode length, format, where people listen and what they'd cut. Listeners who rate the show highly are asked which episode stuck with them, and anyone less keen is asked what would win them back.

preview.greeting: Hey, thanks for listening! Got three minutes to help us plan the next season?
preview.question: How long have you been listening?

templates.title: Presentation feedback survey
templates.description: Hear whether the audience could follow the talk and how the delivery landed.
templates.metaDescription: Ask your audience if they could follow the talk, whether it delivered what it promised and how the delivery landed, in the room or online. Replies go to the speaker.
templates.blurb: Built around the question speakers rarely ask: how much of it could you follow? Anyone who lost the thread is asked where, people who watched online are asked about sound and slides, and anyone with an unanswered question can ask the speaker for a reply and reach their own ending.

preview.greeting: Thanks for coming to the talk. Two minutes of honest feedback would help the speaker a lot.
preview.question: Which talk or session are you giving feedback on?
preview.next: How did you watch it?

templates.title: Pricing survey
templates.description: Find out whether your price is clear, feels fair and holds up against the alternatives.
templates.metaDescription: Find out how buyers read your pricing: their first reaction, what was hard to work out, whether it feels fair and what they compared it with before deciding.
templates.blurb: Focuses on how the price is presented and judged rather than on the number alone. People who found the pricing confusing are asked exactly what was hard to work out, anyone who thinks it's too high is asked what would make it worth paying, and everyone says what they compared you with.

preview.greeting: We're reviewing how we price and explain what we sell. Could you give us three minutes?
preview.question: Where are you with us right now?

templates.title: Process improvement survey
templates.description: Find the friction in a workflow by asking the people who do the work.
templates.metaDescription: Ask the people who run a process where time is lost, what goes wrong and which fixes would help most. Workarounds and follow-up offers get their own questions.
templates.blurb: Asks about one named process, so answers stay concrete. It collects the last real mistake, the workarounds people have built for themselves and a ranked list of fixes, and anyone willing to talk it through leaves an email and reaches a separate sign-off.

preview.greeting: You know this process better than anyone. Help us find what's slowing it down? About four minutes.
preview.question: Which process are you giving feedback on?
preview.next: What's your part in it?

templates.title: Program satisfaction survey
templates.description: Hear how participants found a program, including the ones who didn't finish.
templates.metaDescription: Ask participants if a program met their needs, which parts helped and what got in the way. People who left early are asked why, so you hear from them too.
templates.blurb: Works for training courses, mentoring schemes, community programs and more. It asks where each person is in the program, so someone who left early is asked why before rating the parts they did use. Participants who want to hear about the next stage leave an email and get their own sign-off.

preview.greeting: Thanks for taking part in the program. Could you tell us how it's going? It takes about four minutes.
preview.question: Which program did you take part in?
preview.next: Where are you in the program?

templates.title: Quality assurance review
templates.description: Log each quality review the same way, from checks done to fixes assigned.
templates.metaDescription: A QA review for reviewers to record what they checked, the result and any issues found. Failed checks capture severity, evidence, a fix owner and a due date.
templates.blurb: Gives every reviewer the same checklist, whether they're checking a product batch, a support conversation or a document. A pass goes straight to the closing notes, while anything with issues asks for severity and evidence, and corrective action gets an owner and a due date.

preview.greeting: Ready to log a quality review? Have the item and your notes to hand.
preview.question: Reviewer name
preview.next: Date of the review

templates.title: Team retrospective
templates.description: Collect everyone's view of a sprint or project before the retro meeting.
templates.metaDescription: Gather each person's view before the team retro: what went well, what slowed you down, how the team did against last time and one thing to try next.
templates.blurb: Filled in privately before the meeting, so quieter people get heard and the discussion starts from real answers. It compares this period with the last one, asks for one concrete thing to try, and anyone who didn't feel safe raising problems gets a gentle follow-up question.

preview.greeting: Retro time. Answer on your own before we meet, so we can spend the meeting on what matters.
preview.question: Which sprint, project or period is this for?
preview.next: How did this stretch of work feel for you?

templates.title: Skin care survey
templates.description: Learn how people care for their skin and what makes them choose a product.
