templates.metaDescription: Ask customers about their skin type, routine, goals and what they look for when choosing products. People keen to test new products can sign up at the end.
templates.blurb: Built for skincare brands and shops researching their customers, not for diagnosis. It asks about routine, goals and buying habits, gives anyone who's had a reaction a place to describe it, and invites adults who want to test new products to leave an email for a product-testing ending. Anyone under 18 skips the tester invitation.

preview.greeting: Tell us about your skincare routine? It takes about three minutes, and this isn't a skin assessment, just your habits and preferences.
preview.question: How would you describe your skin most days?

templates.title: Social media survey
templates.description: Learn where your audience spends time online and what they want to see from you there.
templates.metaDescription: Ask your audience which platforms they use, which formats and topics help them, and what makes them unfollow. Followers and non-followers get different questions.
templates.blurb: Starts with the platforms people actually use, then splits: people who already follow you say why and how useful your posts are, and people who don't say what has kept them away. Everyone then ranks formats, picks topics and names what makes them unfollow an account.

preview.greeting: We're planning what to post next and would rather ask than guess. Two or three minutes, and every answer shapes what you'll see from us.
preview.question: Which of these do you use at least once a week?

templates.title: Sustainability survey
templates.description: Find out which green changes your customers care about and what gets in the way of choosing them.
templates.metaDescription: Ask customers which sustainability changes matter, what they already do, what stops them and which claims they trust. People who know your efforts get to rate them.
templates.blurb: Asks about everyday habits and obstacles before any talk of your own plans, so the answers aren't shaped by what people think you want to hear. Only customers who already know about your efforts are asked to rate them; everyone ranks the changes they'd value most and says what would make a green claim believable.

preview.greeting: We're deciding which changes to make first to reduce our environmental impact, and we'd like your view. It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: When you choose where to buy, how much does a company's environmental impact matter to you?
preview.next: Which of these do you already do most of the time?

templates.title: Target market survey
templates.description: Test who needs what you're building, before you decide which audience to focus on.
templates.metaDescription: Find out who has the problem your product solves, how badly, and how they deal with it now. People without the problem are screened out; keen ones can offer to talk.
templates.blurb: Starts with how often the problem comes up, and anyone who doesn't have it explains why and leaves early instead of padding your data. Everyone else rates the pain, describes their current fix, says who decides and what they'd judge a new option on, and can volunteer for a follow-up conversation.

preview.greeting: We're working on a way to make keeping track of household bills less of a chore, and we're trying to learn who struggles with it most. About three minutes.
preview.question: Who would you be solving this for?

templates.title: Technology survey
templates.description: Understand how people use technology at work, where it slows them down and what support they need.
templates.metaDescription: Ask your team which tools they rely on, how confident they feel, how much time tech problems cost them and how they like to learn before you roll out a change.
templates.blurb: A workplace technology check that goes past a satisfaction score. People rate each part of their setup, say how much time they lose each week, and only those losing real time are asked to describe the problem. It ends on how they feel about new tools and how they'd like to learn one, which is what you need before any change.

preview.greeting: We're reviewing the tools and devices people use at work. Tell us what helps and what gets in the way. It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: Which team are you in?

templates.title: Training evaluation
templates.description: Find out how well a training session was designed and delivered, and what to change for the next group.
templates.metaDescription: Rate a training session on clarity, relevance, practice time, pace, level and delivery. Anyone who wouldn't recommend it as it stands says what should change.
templates.blurb: Written for the people who run the training. It rates the parts you can change, from objectives and examples to practice time, pace and level, then asks whether the learner would recommend the session. A yes leads to what worked best; anything less leads to what would need to change first.

preview.greeting: Thanks for taking part. A few quick questions about how the session was run, so the next group gets a better one.
preview.question: Which session did you attend?
preview.next: Overall, how would you rate the session?

templates.title: User satisfaction survey
templates.description: Learn how well your product works for the people using it, and the reason behind each score.
templates.metaDescription: Ask users what they were trying to do, whether they managed it and why they gave their score. People who struggled or gave up get their own follow-up questions.
templates.blurb: Anchors every answer to a real task instead of a general impression. Users who finished easily move straight to the rating, users who struggled say what made it hard, and users who gave up say where it broke and what they did instead. Each score comes with a reason, and the AI follow-up asks for more when that reason is vague.

preview.greeting: We'd like to know how using our product is going for you. Five minutes at most, and your answers go straight to the team building it.
preview.question: The last time you used it, what were you trying to get done?
preview.next: Did you manage it?

templates.title: Value proposition test
templates.description: Test whether your offer's promise is understood, relevant and believable before you build a campaign on it.
templates.metaDescription: Show people your offer's promise, then ask what they think it does, which benefit matters, how believable it is and what would convince them. Poor fits leave early.
templates.blurb: Shows the promise, then asks people to explain it back in their own words, which catches confusing messaging faster than any rating. Anyone for whom it isn't relevant says who it would suit and leaves. The rest rank the benefits, score how believable the claim is, name their doubts and say what proof would win them over.

preview.greeting: We're testing how we describe something new, and we'd value your honest first reaction. About three minutes.
preview.question: In your own words, what does this offer do, and who is it for?
preview.next: How clear was that description?

templates.title: Vendor satisfaction survey
templates.description: Hear how suppliers experience working with your organisation, and fix what makes you a hard customer.
templates.metaDescription: Ask suppliers how working with you really goes: orders, replies, forecasts, paperwork and payment on time. Late-payment problems and call requests get follow-ups.
templates.blurb: Turns the usual supplier review around so vendors rate you. They score the parts of the relationship you control, and anyone who says invoices are often paid late is asked what holds them up. It finishes with what would help most and an offer of a call with your purchasing team, which gets its own ending.

preview.greeting: We rely on our suppliers, and we'd like to be a customer that's easy to work with. Tell us honestly how we're doing. About four minutes.
preview.question: Which company are you answering for?
preview.next: How long have you been supplying us?

templates.title: Website UX survey
templates.description: Find out where your website helps visitors finish a task and where it lets them down.
templates.metaDescription: Ask visitors what they came to do on your website and whether they managed it. People who got stuck say where and what happened; everyone rates speed and navigation.
templates.blurb: Built around one real visit rather than general opinions. Visitors who got what they came for rate how easy it was; anyone who got stuck picks where it went wrong and describes what happened, which is the detail a designer can use. Everyone then says how they looked for things and rates navigation, speed and readability on the device they used.

preview.greeting: Quick question about your visit today: did our website help you do what you came for? It takes two minutes.
preview.question: What did you come to the site to do?
preview.answer: Learn about a product or service

templates.title: Workshop feedback
templates.description: Learn what participants took from a hands-on session and what support they need afterwards.
templates.metaDescription: Ask participants which activities helped, whether the pace and balance of practice worked and how ready they feel to go it alone. Unsure ones pick the help needed.
templates.blurb: Made for practical sessions where people learn by doing. It rates each activity, checks the pace and the balance of explaining versus practising, then asks how ready people feel to try it alone. Confident participants name what they'll do first; hesitant ones pick the support that would help, so you know what to send afterwards.

preview.greeting: Thanks for joining the workshop. A few quick questions while it's fresh, so we can make the next one better. About three minutes.
preview.question: Which workshop did you take part in?
preview.next: Overall, how would you rate it?

templates.title: Brand perception
templates.description: Learn the words people attach to your brand, and the experiences behind them.
templates.metaDescription: Find out what people really think of your brand: the words they pick, how far they trust you and how you compare. Non-buyers skip the questions they can't answer.
templates.blurb: Asks how well someone knows you before asking what they think, so the answers can be split by customers, lapsed customers and people who have only heard of you. Anyone who has never bought skips the experience grid and goes straight to how you compare, and anyone whose view has shifted is asked what shifted it.

preview.greeting: We're trying to see ourselves the way you see us. Five minutes, and honest answers help most.
preview.question: How well do you know us?

templates.title: Brand personality
templates.description: See whether the personality people feel matches the one you meant to build.
templates.metaDescription: Ask customers what kind of person your brand would be: its traits, its tone and where it sits between serious and playful. Compare that with the voice you intended.
templates.blurb: Uses sliders between opposite traits, like serious and playful or traditional and modern, so you get positions you can compare with your brand guidelines rather than a pile of adjectives. Anyone who feels your words and your actions don't match is asked where the gap shows up.

preview.greeting: Quick one: if our brand were a person, what would they be like? No right answers here.
preview.question: How do you know us?

templates.title: Business impact
templates.description: See how a change is really landing, team by team, and what support would help.
templates.metaDescription: Measure how a change is affecting daily work: workload, speed, quality and customers. People hit hardest describe the disruption and name the support they need.
templates.blurb: Built for the weeks after a reorganisation, a new system, a price change or an outside event. A grid rates the effect on workload, speed, quality, customers and costs, and the overall verdict decides the follow-up: people seeing gains describe them, people struggling describe the disruption, and everyone picks the support that would help.

preview.greeting: We want to understand how the recent change is affecting your work. It takes about four minutes.
preview.question: Which change are you telling us about?
preview.next: Which team or area do you work in?

templates.title: Churn survey
templates.description: Learn why customers left or went quiet, and when the product stopped being worth it.
templates.metaDescription: Find out why customers stopped using your product, whether they cancelled or drifted away. Each reason gets its own follow-up, then ask what would win them back.
templates.blurb: Works for people who cancelled and for people who simply stopped using you, and asks when the product stopped feeling worth it so you can see where value falls away. Every reason gets its own follow-up: a cheaper option, the missing feature, the competitor and why, what got in the way, what changed in their needs or what kept it out of their routine. Only people open to coming back are asked what it would take and for an email.

preview.greeting: We noticed you've stepped away, and we'd like to understand why. It takes two minutes and shapes what we fix next.
preview.question: Which of these fits you best?

templates.title: Client questionnaire
templates.description: Understand a client's goals and context before you recommend anything.
templates.metaDescription: Learn a new client's goals, challenges, budget and deadline before your first call. Ask who you'll work with day to day, and what success would look like to them.
templates.blurb: Covers what you need before a discovery call: who you'll work with, what the business does, what success looks like, what's in the way and what has been tried. If the person filling it in isn't the day-to-day contact, it asks who is, and a budget amount is only requested from clients who already have one in mind.

preview.greeting: Looking forward to working together. A few questions first, so our first call can get straight to the useful part.
preview.question: Let's start with you. Who are we talking to?
preview.next: What's the name of your business?

templates.title: Conference evaluation
templates.description: Hear what attendees valued and what to change before next year's conference.
templates.metaDescription: Rate your conference: sessions, networking, venue and value. Happy attendees name their highlight, unhappy ones say what went wrong, and everyone suggests topics.
templates.blurb: Asks for the overall verdict first, then follows it: attendees who loved it name their highlight, and those who didn't say what let them down. A grid rates keynotes, breakouts, networking, venue, food and scheduling, so you can separate a strong programme from a weak venue. It also asks what attendees will use at work and how many useful contacts they made, the two things most people go to a conference for, and closes with topics for next year.

preview.greeting: Thanks for coming to the conference. Tell us how it went for you, and help shape the next one.
preview.question: How did you take part?

templates.title: Consumer behavior
templates.description: Understand real buying decisions by asking about one recent purchase.
templates.metaDescription: Study how people really shop by walking through a recent purchase: what set it off, where they looked, what decided it and how they feel about it now.
templates.blurb: Anchored on one real, recent purchase instead of general shopping habits, so answers describe what people did rather than what they think they do. It follows the purchase from trigger to research to the deciding factor, skips the comparison question for people who didn't shop around, and asks less happy buyers what they would do differently.

preview.greeting: We're studying how people make buying decisions. Think of one recent purchase and we'll walk through it together.
preview.question: Think of the last thing you bought that took some thought, not an everyday top-up. What was it?
preview.next: When did you buy it?

templates.title: Consumer preferences
templates.description: Find out which features matter, which trade-offs people accept, and what makes them switch.
templates.metaDescription: Learn what your audience values in a product and which trade-offs they'll accept. Rank features, find deal-breakers and see what would make people switch brands.
templates.blurb: Goes past 'what do you like' to the choices that shape a product: a ranking of priorities, a grid that separates nice-to-haves from deal-breakers, and direct trade-off questions on price and sustainability. People who wouldn't switch from their current brand are asked what keeps them loyal, and everyone else describes the product they'd switch for.

preview.greeting: We're designing something new and want it to fit how you actually choose. A few quick questions.
preview.question: How often do you buy or use this kind of product?

templates.title: CSR survey
templates.description: Learn which causes matter to your people and whether your current efforts feel real.
templates.metaDescription: Ask employees, customers and partners which social and environmental issues matter, what they know of your efforts and whether they believe them. Plan CSR with it.
templates.blurb: Separates three things that usually get mixed up: how much people care, how much they know about what you already do, and whether they believe it. People who know nothing about your work skip the credibility question, and people who find your efforts unconvincing are asked what would change their mind.

preview.greeting: We're deciding where to focus our social and environmental work, and we'd like your view. About four minutes.
preview.question: What's your connection to us?

templates.title: Customer analysis
templates.description: Understand who buys from you, what problem they had and why they chose you.
templates.metaDescription: Learn who your customers are and why they buy: their situation, the problem they had, the options they weighed and why they chose you. For B2B and consumer buyers.
templates.blurb: Starts by asking whether the customer bought for themselves or for a business, then asks the background questions that fit: company size and role for business buyers, age range for everyone else. After that everyone describes the problem they had, the alternatives they weighed and the real reason they chose you.

preview.greeting: Thanks for being a customer. We'd love to understand you a little better. It takes about four minutes.
preview.question: Did you buy from us for yourself or for work?

templates.title: Customer attitudes
templates.description: See how customers feel about your product, with the reasons behind every rating.
templates.metaDescription: Measure how customers feel about your product and why. Positive, neutral and negative customers each get their own follow-up, then all rate five statements.
templates.blurb: Asks for a feeling first, then the reason behind it, with a different follow-up for positive, lukewarm and negative customers. A grid of agree-or-disagree statements covers value, trust, ease of use and how you compare, and a closing question on how views have shifted shows whether things are heading the right way.

preview.greeting: We'd like to hear how you honestly feel about our product. It takes about three minutes.
preview.question: How long have you been using our product?

templates.title: Happiness check-in
templates.description: A quick, honest check-in on how people feel, with a private follow-up for anyone who asks.
templates.metaDescription: A short happiness check-in for a team, program or community. Tracks mood over time, asks what is changing it, and offers a private follow-up to anyone who wants one.
templates.blurb: A happiness survey that asks why, not just how much. People who say they are less happy than before are asked what changed, people doing well are asked what is working, and anyone can ask for a private conversation without putting their name on every answer.

preview.greeting: Hi! This is a quick check-in on how you're feeling here lately. It takes about three minutes, and there are no wrong answers.
preview.question: Over the past month, how happy have you felt here?
preview.next: Compared with a few months ago, is that...

templates.title: Political opinion survey
templates.description: Ask people where they stand on public issues, in neutral wording that leaves room for every view.
templates.metaDescription: A neutral political survey on public issues. Ranks what people care about, measures trust and priorities, and asks those unhappy with the direction why.
templates.blurb: Built for researchers, student groups, local organisations and campaigns who want honest answers rather than the ones a leading question produces. Every question has a balanced set of options, people who think things are on the wrong track are asked why, and the demographic questions are optional and come last.

preview.greeting: Hi! We're asking people in the area about the public issues that matter to them. It takes about four minutes, and every view is welcome.
preview.question: Which town, city or area do you live in?
preview.next: In general, do you think things in your area are heading in the right direction or on the wrong track?

templates.title: User persona research
templates.description: Gather the goals, habits and frustrations you need to build personas from real answers.
templates.metaDescription: Collect the goals, daily tasks, current tools and frustrations that shape your users, then invite the most useful respondents to a follow-up interview.
templates.blurb: Personas are only as good as the answers behind them, so this survey asks about what people actually do rather than what they would like. It covers role, goals, how often the task comes up, today's tools and what makes people switch, then routes anyone willing to talk to an interview sign-up.

preview.greeting: Hi! We're trying to understand the people we build for. A few questions about your work and how you get it done, about four minutes.
preview.question: Which of these best describes your role?

templates.title: Performance review input
templates.description: Gather input from the people who work with someone, ahead of their performance review.
templates.metaDescription: Collect input on one employee from their manager and colleagues before a review: goals, a standout piece of work, core skills and one specific thing to improve.
templates.blurb: A survey the people around an employee fill in, so the review draws on more than one view. Only their manager is asked about agreed goals, a missed goal gets asked what got in the way, and everyone gives a real work example, rates the same skills and names one specific thing to improve.

preview.greeting: Hi! You've been asked for input on a colleague's performance ahead of their review. It takes about five minutes, and specific examples help far more than general praise or criticism.
preview.question: Whose performance are you giving input on?
preview.next: How do you work with them?

templates.title: Performance process review
templates.description: Find out whether your goals, feedback and reviews actually help people do better work.
templates.metaDescription: Ask staff whether your goal setting, feedback and review process helps them improve. Managers get their own questions, and a low score asks what isn't working.
templates.blurb: A survey about the performance process itself, not anyone's performance. Managers are asked what would help them run better reviews, everyone rates how clear, fair and useful the process is, and anyone who rates it 3 or below is asked where it lets them down so you know what to fix first.

preview.greeting: Hi! We want to know whether the way we set goals, give feedback and run reviews is actually helping. This is about the process, not your performance, and it takes about four minutes.
preview.question: Do you manage other people?

templates.title: Work-life balance survey
templates.description: See where workload and boundaries are slipping, and which support would help most.
templates.metaDescription: Understand how work fits with life outside it: hours, after-hours contact, boundaries and flexibility. Low scores get asked what's making balance hardest.
templates.blurb: Covers the practical things that decide balance: hours, how often work spills into evenings, whether people can switch off and use their leave. Anyone who rates their balance low is asked what's making it hardest, and everyone ranks the kinds of flexibility that would help them most.

preview.greeting: Hi! We want to understand how work fits with the rest of your life, and what would make it fit better. About four minutes, and your answers are anonymous.
preview.question: How do you mostly work at the moment?

templates.title: Training needs assessment
templates.description: Find the real skill gaps and preferred formats before you spend a training budget.
templates.metaDescription: Find skill gaps before you plan training. Staff rate their confidence on key skills, describe where they got stuck, and pick the formats and topics that would help.
templates.blurb: A needs assessment that asks about real work, not wish lists. People rate their confidence on the skills their job depends on, describe a recent moment where more training would have helped, and rank how they like to learn. Anyone confident enough to teach a topic is asked what they could share.

preview.greeting: Hi! We're planning training for the months ahead and want it to fit the work you really do. It takes about five minutes.
preview.question: Which team or department are you in?
preview.next: How long have you been in your current role?

templates.title: Training satisfaction
templates.description: Hear how a training session landed, and which part lifted or sank the overall score.
templates.metaDescription: Find out how satisfied people were with a training session, from content and trainer to materials and setup, and what lifted or lowered their overall rating.
templates.blurb: A satisfaction survey that pins the overall score to a cause. A high rating asks which part made the session, a lower one asks what let it down and what would have fixed it, and everyone rates their satisfaction with the content, trainer, materials, length and setup.

preview.greeting: Thanks for taking part in the training! Two or three minutes of feedback helps us make the next session better.
preview.question: Which training session did you attend?
preview.next: How did you take part?

templates.title: Commuting survey
templates.description: Learn how people travel in, what it costs them and what would make the trip easier.
templates.metaDescription: Find out how people get to work or study: how often, how long, by what means and what gets in the way. Unhappy commuters are asked what makes the trip hard.
templates.blurb: A travel survey for employers, campuses and site managers planning parking, flexible hours or transport support. People who never travel in are thanked and let go at the first question, and anyone who rates their commute poorly is asked what makes it hard before everyone ranks the changes that would help most.

preview.greeting: We're planning how to make getting here easier. Tell us about your usual journey in; it takes about two minutes.
preview.question: In a typical week, how many days do you travel in?

templates.title: Market research survey
templates.description: Test a market before you build or sell: the problem, the alternatives and the buying criteria.
templates.metaDescription: Explore a market before you commit: the problem people have, how they solve it today, what they pay and what would put them off. Screens out the wrong people.
templates.blurb: Written around a real example, weekly meal planning, so you can see how good market research questions sound before swapping in your own market. People who aren't the decision maker are screened out politely, those who already pay for a solution are asked what they bought, and only volunteers are asked for an email.

preview.greeting: We're researching how households plan and cook their weekly meals. It takes about three minutes, and there are no right answers.
preview.question: Who usually decides what gets cooked in your home?

templates.title: Product research survey
templates.description: Understand the task, the current workaround and the unsolved problems before you build.
templates.metaDescription: Learn how people do a task today, the tools they use and where it breaks, before you design a product. Asks why they abandoned past tools and who will try a beta.
templates.blurb: Built around one example task, sending invoices, to show how product research questions work: the last time they did it, the tools they use, and a grid of which problems are real. People who never do the task are thanked and let go, anyone who gave up on a tool is asked why, and only willing testers leave an email.

preview.greeting: We're trying to understand how people handle invoicing before we build anything. It's about four minutes, and honest answers help most.
preview.question: Which best describes your work?

templates.title: Candidate experience survey
templates.description: Hear from applicants about your job ads, interviews and communication, at every stage.
templates.metaDescription: Ask applicants how your hiring process felt: the job ad, the interviews, how fast you replied and whether they felt respected, whatever the outcome.
templates.blurb: One survey for every applicant, whether they were hired or not. People who only applied skip the interview questions, and anyone who didn't feel treated with respect is asked what happened, so the complaints worth acting on come with detail.

preview.greeting: Thanks for applying to work with us. Whatever the outcome, we'd value two minutes of honest feedback on how our process felt.
preview.question: Which role did you apply for?
preview.next: How clearly did the job ad describe the role and what it would involve?

templates.title: Job satisfaction survey
templates.description: Measure how people feel about the job itself, with a different follow-up for low and high scores.
templates.metaDescription: Ask employees how they feel about the work, their workload, pay, recognition and growth. Low scorers are asked what's wrong; high scorers what's worth protecting.
templates.blurb: Covers the parts of a job that shape how people feel about it, from the work itself to recognition and room to grow. The overall score decides the follow-up: someone struggling is asked what's making the job hard, someone content is asked what's worth protecting, and everyone says whether they see themselves here in a year.

preview.greeting: This survey is about how your job feels right now. It takes about three minutes, and answers are reported only as team totals.
preview.question: Which part of the organisation do you work in?

templates.title: Performance appraisal
templates.description: Help employees prepare for their review with goals, examples, a self-rating and next steps.
templates.metaDescription: A self-appraisal employees fill in before their review: goals met, work they're proud of, a self-rating, support needed and goals for the next period.
templates.blurb: Sent before a review meeting so the conversation starts from the employee's own account. Anyone who met only some of their goals is asked what got in the way before sharing their best work, and it ends with the support they need and the goals they'd set next, so the meeting can move straight to agreeing a plan.

preview.greeting: Your review is coming up. This helps you and your manager start from the same page, and takes about ten minutes to answer thoughtfully.
preview.question: What's your name?
preview.next: What's your current job title?

templates.title: Supervisor evaluation
templates.description: Anonymous feedback from shift and frontline teams on how their supervisor runs the shift.
templates.metaDescription: Let shift and frontline teams rate day-to-day supervision: clear instructions, fair shifts, handovers and coaching on the job, plus how mistakes get handled.
templates.blurb: Built for shift-based and frontline teams, where supervision is about the shift in front of you: clear instructions, fair rotas, proper handovers and help on the job. Anyone whose supervisor blames people or stays out of it when something goes wrong is asked for an example, which is often the most useful answer in the whole survey.

preview.greeting: Tell us how supervision works on your shifts. It's anonymous and takes about three minutes.
preview.question: Who is the supervisor you're giving feedback on?
preview.next: Which shift do you usually work with them?

templates.title: Demographic questionnaire
templates.description: Background questions for research, with consent first and a way to skip anything personal.
templates.metaDescription: Collect respondent background for research: age, gender, location, education, work and household, with a prefer-not-to-say option and consent asked up front.
templates.blurb: A set of respectful demographic questions to add to research or use on its own, with consent asked first and a 'prefer not to say' on every sensitive question. Anyone under 18 is stopped at the age question and let go kindly, so you don't collect data you shouldn't from minors.

preview.greeting: A few questions about you. They help us understand who took part, and you can skip anything you'd rather not share.
preview.question: How we'll use your answers
preview.next: How old are you?

templates.title: Concept test
templates.description: Check whether an early idea is understood, wanted and worth building.
templates.metaDescription: Show people an early idea and learn what they think it does, whether they have the problem, and what worries them. Keen testers can join an early access list.
templates.blurb: The concept is shown first, then people explain it back in their own words, so you learn whether the idea is clear before you read a single rating. Anyone who rarely has the problem skips the questions about how they solve it today, and people who say they would try it are offered early access while the rest are asked what would change their mind.

preview.greeting: We're working on a new idea and would love your honest first impressions. It takes about four minutes.
preview.question: What's your first reaction?
preview.next: In a sentence or two, what do you think this does?

templates.title: Focus group survey
templates.description: Hear from every participant before and after the group discussion, not just the loudest.
templates.metaDescription: One survey for both sides of a focus group: capture each participant's views before the session, then what they held back and what changed their mind after it.
templates.blurb: The first question asks whether the session is still ahead or already over, and each group gets its own set of questions. Before the session you learn each person's starting view and what they want to discuss; afterwards you learn what they did not get to say and whether the discussion changed their mind.

preview.greeting: Thanks for taking part in our focus group. A few questions on your own first, so every view gets heard.
preview.question: What's your first name?
preview.next: Is the session still ahead of you, or has it already happened?

templates.title: New product survey
templates.description: Learn who wants your new product, what matters to them and what's stopping them.
templates.metaDescription: Test a product before launch: how often people face the problem, which features matter, what they'd expect to pay and what they need to know before trying it.
templates.blurb: People who never have the problem are thanked and let go straight away, so your numbers come from the audience you're actually building for. Everyone else ranks the features, names a price and says what they'd need to know first, and the ones planning to try it can leave an email for the launch.

preview.greeting: We're getting ready to launch something new and want to build it around what you actually need. About four minutes.
preview.question: How often do you run into the problem this product is built to solve?

templates.title: Product satisfaction
templates.description: Find out whether the product lived up to what buyers expected, and why.
templates.metaDescription: Ask buyers how well your product lived up to expectations, rate quality, ease of use and value, and offer to follow up with anyone it let down.
templates.blurb: One question splits the survey: did the product turn out better, about the same or worse than expected? Buyers it pleased say what they like most, and buyers it disappointed say what fell short and can ask to be contacted so you can put it right.

preview.greeting: Thanks for your purchase. Now that you've had some time with it, how is it going?
preview.question: Which product are you reviewing?
preview.next: How long have you been using it?

templates.title: Product testing survey
templates.description: Find out what testers tried, where they struggled and what they expected instead.
templates.metaDescription: Collect what happened when testers tried your product: whether they finished the task, where they got stuck, what they expected and any bugs they hit.
templates.blurb: Anchored to the task you set: testers who finished easily move on, testers who struggled say which step was hardest, and testers who got stuck say where and can attach a screenshot. Everyone then says what they expected to happen, rates ease and quality, and reports any bugs they spotted.

preview.greeting: Thanks for testing for us. Tell us what happened while it's fresh; the problems are the most useful part.
preview.question: What's your name or tester ID?
preview.next: What did you test it on?

templates.title: Product-market fit survey
templates.description: The disappointment question, a different follow-up for each answer, and who your fans are.
templates.metaDescription: Measure product-market fit with the 'how disappointed would you be' question, then a different follow-up for each answer, plus alternatives and where it falls short.
templates.blurb: Asks how disappointed people would be if the product disappeared, then gives each answer its own conversation: fans describe the benefit in their own words, the somewhat disappointed say what's missing, and the rest say why it isn't useful. Everyone then names their alternative and where it falls short, and the role and team questions show who your fans are.

preview.greeting: A few questions about how you use us. Honest answers help most, including critical ones.
preview.question: How often do you use the product?

templates.title: Sean Ellis test
templates.description: The four classic Sean Ellis questions, asked only of people who have really used the product.
templates.metaDescription: Run the Sean Ellis test the standard way: screen for recent users, ask the four core questions and invite your most engaged fans to a follow-up interview.
templates.blurb: Keeps the standard Sean Ellis questions and asks them of everyone in the same order, so your result is comparable from one round to the next. A first question thanks and releases people who have barely used the product, and anyone happy to talk more can leave an email for a follow-up interview.

preview.greeting: We'd love your honest take on the product. A handful of short questions, about two minutes.
preview.question: How much have you used the product recently?
preview.answer: Regularly in the past couple of weeks

templates.title: Student demographics
templates.description: Background questions that help you plan support, each one optional and easy to skip.
templates.metaDescription: Learn the make-up of your student group: study mode, age, first-generation status, work and caring duties, with every personal question optional and easy to skip.
templates.blurb: Sticks to background that changes how you plan: how people study, whether they work or care for someone, and whether they are first in their family to study at this level. Every sensitive question is optional with a prefer-not-to-say answer, and anyone who would like a word with student support can ask for one at the end.

preview.greeting: Welcome! A few quick questions about you help us plan support that fits. Everything personal is optional.
preview.question: Which course or programme are you on?
preview.next: Which year of study are you in?

templates.title: Student wellbeing check-in
templates.description: A short, kind check-in that lets students ask for support without having to say it out loud.
templates.metaDescription: A gentle check-in on how students are feeling: mood, sleep, workload, belonging and what's weighing on them, with a clear way to ask to talk to someone.

templates.title: Pétanque boule finder
templates.description: Send leisure players to a garden set and match club players to boules for pointing or shooting.
templates.metaDescription: Help players choose pétanque boules. Casual players get a garden or beach set, and club players are matched on hand size, grip and whether they point or shoot.
templates.blurb: Splits early between people playing for fun and people playing in a club, because they need different boules. Leisure players are asked where and with whom they play, while club players answer about hand size, grip and weight before their playing position picks a pointer, shooter or all-round result.

preview.greeting: Choosing pétanque boules? A few questions about how you play and we'll suggest the right set.
preview.question: How long have you been playing?

templates.title: Bridal accessories finder
templates.description: Match accessories to the dress, hair and wedding style, then suggest a coordinated look.
templates.metaDescription: Help brides choose a veil, headpiece and jewellery that suit the dress, hair and wedding style. Their style leads to one of four coordinated looks.
templates.blurb: Asks about the dress first, because neckline and detail decide most accessory choices, then hair, metals, comfort and what's still missing. The bride's overall style picks one of four coordinated looks, and her wedding date and budget go to your dashboard for the follow-up.

preview.greeting: Congratulations! Let's find the finishing touches for your wedding look.

templates.title: Bridesmaid dress finder
templates.description: Suggest matching, same-colour or mix-and-match dresses for the whole bridal party.
templates.metaDescription: Help a bridal party choose a bridesmaid dress approach from wedding style, colours, fit needs and budget, then suggest matching, same-colour or mixed dresses.
templates.blurb: Collects what a bridal stylist needs before an appointment: the date, how many bridesmaids, the wedding style, colours, length and fit needs across the group. The answer about how matched the party should look sends them to one of three approaches, with a clear suggestion for anyone still unsure.

preview.greeting: Dressing the bridal party? Let's work out an approach that looks great and works for everyone.
